units.translation: How cruelly the divinity has entered the race of the Persians.
Whom now the divinity has shorn.
For this divinity, again, has turned against me.
A divinity heavy with wrath falling upon.
The divinity laughs at a hot-tempered man.
Struck by the heavy bile of a divinity, to our misfortune.
And the divinity that is unconquerable, unwarlike, unholy.
Calling upon the three-cubit divinity of this family.
You praise a great divinity for this house, and one heavy in wrath.
O divinity hard to deal with.
Divinity, who falls upon the house.

In Homer δήϊος [hostile]; but the tragedians, like γάϊος [of the earth] and νάϊος [of a ship], also said δάϊος (contracted to δᾷος in Aeschylus in the places indicated below and in the compound δαϊόφρων [hostile-minded]), but they kept the Ionic letter in ἀδῇος δηοῦν δηάλωτος [unhostile, to ravage, capturable]. Its meaning among them is twofold: hostile and wretched. Examples of the former in Aeschylus are
The other meaning is wretched, ruined.
Thus from the copy (δαΐαν [hostile]) for δίαν [divine].
In the sense of formidable (as Hesychius explains δαΐα [hostile] by φοβερά [fearful]) it is said
In the plural number δάϊοι [hostile ones] used substantively means enemies.
Of hostile men (thus I wrote for δηίων [of enemies]) against the walls.
Against a man hostile (δηΐοισιν Μ [hostile in M]) in wrath, reverence.
A marriage that is ill for the husband, hostile.
In every way ward off the capture by enemies.
Wretched, all-daring mother, in wretched funeral rites you dared to lay out your husband without lamentation.
(contracted from Δάειρα [Daeira], on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 847) is a name of Proserpina, on which see schol. Apoll. Rh. 3, 847, whose words we have quoted in fr. 275.

Of this word only two cases are in use, δαΐ [in battle] and δάϊν [battle (accusative)]: on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 866. In the dative after Homer, who said ἐν δαΐ λυγρῇ [in destructive battle], Aeschylus used it
where in several copies δαΐδι [with a torch].
I understood the feast of Thyestes on the flesh of his children.
He provided a feast of children's flesh.
For thus lawful feasts of mortals would be established for you.
of the eagle eating the heart of Prometheus
Uninvited, creeping, a feaster all day long.
Kindling fire and light for freedom.
And you will feast on me alive.
to bite oneself, to torment oneself
(middle form) I bite myself, I torment myself.
It is attributed improperly to things.
